newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesians go on trial on subversion charges.
newsitem.headline: Indonesians go on trial on subversion charges.

text.p: Three Indonesian activists went on trial in Surabaya on Monday accused of spreading hatred against the government and subversion, which carries the death penalty.
Prosecutors also accused them of involvement in labour protests in Indonesia's second city, in East Java.
Dita Indah Sari, 23, and Coen Husein Pontoh, 26, were being tried together, while Mochamad Sholeh, 21, faced a separate trial in Surabaya State Court which opened amid tight security.
All three were arrested after a mass strike involving thousands of workers from 10 different companies in Surabaya on July 8 which prosecutors alleged was led by Sari and Pontoh.

"(Sari) spoke at the protest and called for an increased minimum wage of 7,000 rupiah ($3.00) as well as an end to certain political laws, army interference in labour disputes and the army's socio-political role," prosecutor Septinus Hematang said.

Prosecutors said the three were affiliated with the small left-wing People's Democratic Party (PRD) which was subversive because it did not take the state ideology as its sole basis of association as required by law.
The state ideology, Pancasila, proclaims belief in one supreme God, justice and civility, the unity of Indonesia, consensus democracy and social justice.

Prosecutors told the court Sari was head of the Indonesian Workers Struggle Centre (PPBI), while Pontoh and Sholeh were officials of Surabaya branches of the Indonesian Farmers Union (STN) and Indonesian Students Solidarity for Democracy (SMID).
All three groups were part of the PRD.

"I understand the contents, but I reject the charges. I did not have the intention to undermine the state. My actions, including involvement in workers' protests, was only to defend workers and the little people," Sari told reporters.
Leading human rights lawyer Adnan Buyung Nasution said the use of the subversion charges was a backwards step.
The subversion trials of another nine activists from the PRD, including its leader Budiman Sudjatmiko, opened in Jakarta on Thursday.
They are also accused of spreading hatred against the government, a law created by the Dutch colonial administration to stifle the nascent independence movement in the 1930s.
